title: The universal subject
summary: Every real sentence has an A-car and a B-engine; when the A-car is not spoken it is a zero pronoun, not a missing subject.

blocks.text: Some teachers say Japanese has no subject, because so many sentences seem to start with nothing. This course disagrees: every real sentence says something (B) about something (A). Japanese is a **null-subject** language, like Spanish: the subject is not always visible, but it is there.
The invisible A-car is found from context, and when context says nothing it defaults to **I**.
It is not that "tiredness hangs over the universe". A language must be able to say B about A.
Some subjects are vague, as English "it" is: 雨になりそうだ, "it looks like rain". The copula だ still needs an A-car, because だ links two things.
A noun with a long modifier is not a sentence:

blocks.en: me, who had arrived at the station

blocks.text: There is no A and B here: just a noun with a modifier. These are used in summaries and narration.

items: Every real sentence has an A-car and a B-engine.
When the A-car is not spoken it is a zero pronoun: context decides, **I** by default.
A noun with a modifier is not a subjectless sentence; it is not a sentence at all.

options: One whose subjects are not always visible
questions.note: The subject is still there.

questions.instruction: In the course's terms だ links an A-car (subject) to a B. Why does 雨になりそうだ still have a hidden A-car?
options: Because だ links an A-car to a B
questions.note: The copula needs two things to link.

questions.instruction: What does the zero pronoun default to in context-free sentences?
questions.note: When nothing else is clear, it is the speaker.

questions.prompt: Japanese has no subject because the subject is often missing.
questions.note: It is often invisible, not absent.

questions.prompt: English also drops the subject in some cases (such as commands).
questions.note: "Stop crying!" has no spoken subject.

questions.instruction: What is this course's view of grammar models?
options: Tools to describe language, not its source code
questions.note: Grammar describes language after the fact.

questions.instruction: Who is sleepy in this sentence said on its own?
questions.note: The invisible A-car defaults to I.

questions.instruction: Who is the zero pronoun here?
questions.prompt: A: 先生は？　B: もう帰りました。
questions.note: Context says A asked about the teacher.
questions.en: A: What about the teacher? B: (He) already went home.

questions.instruction: Which of these is a noun with a modifier, not a sentence?
questions.note: It ends in a noun and says nothing (B) about an A-car.

options: It is a noun with a modifier: it says nothing about an A-car
questions.note: A noun with a modifier has no A and B.
questions.en: the person I met at the station

questions.instruction: Tap the engine (the A-car is a zero pronoun)
questions.note: 行った is the engine; (I) is the invisible A-car.
妹が is the A-car; 来た is the engine.

questions.prompt: 眠い。 This sentence has no A-car (subject) at all, not even an invisible one.
questions.note: The A-car is a zero pronoun, invisible but present.

questions.prompt: お母さんが赤ちゃんを見て、「寝た」と言った。
questions.note: Context fills the zero pronoun: the baby.
questions.en: Mother looked at the baby and said, "(He) fell asleep."

questions.note: Topic, adverb, then the engine; the A-car (I) is zero.

questions.prompt: I went to bed early yesterday.
questions.note: Topic, adverb, engine; (I) is the zero pronoun.
questions.en: I went to bed early yesterday.

questions.instruction: Which sentence has a zero pronoun?
questions.note: Only 早く寝た。 leaves its A-car unspoken.

questions.prompt: 窓を開けた人 is a complete sentence.
questions.note: It is a noun (人) with a modifier.
questions.en: the person who opened the window

questions.prompt: English also uses a vague "it" as a subject, as in "It is raining."
questions.note: Vague subjects exist in many languages.

questions.instruction: Why does this feel complete in Japanese?
options: The zero pronoun (usually I) is the A-car
questions.note: The A-car is invisible but still there.
